opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a meaningful amount. People sometimes assume that because I'm associated with short timelines I think it's basically certain to happen in the next few years, and that's not right. My median has moved around, but I'd still put something like 20 to 30 percent on it taking longer than a decade.

The main ways I see that happening: maybe the current paradigm runs into a wall we don't anticipate. Scaling pre-training gives diminishing returns, the reinforcement learning on top doesn't generalize the way we hope, and we end up with systems that are incredibly impressive at bounded tasks but never get the long-horizon agency, the ability to work autonomously for weeks on a messy real-world project. That's the crux for me. If the time horizon of tasks AIs can do keeps doubling every few months, you get to automating AI research pretty fast, and then things go very quickly. If that trend stalls, the whole picture changes.

There's also a compute-bottleneck story. A lot of the progress has come from spending exponentially more on training runs, and you can't do that forever. At some point you're spending a significant fraction of GDP and it has to slow down. If we haven't hit the critical threshold by then, progress reverts to something more like the pace of algorithmic improvement alone, which is slower. So the probability mass is front-loaded: I think it's fairly likely in the next five years or so, and if it doesn't happen by then, the yearly hazard rate drops.

And then there are things like a major war over Taiwan disrupting chip supply, or serious regulation, which could push things out.

So I don't want to be overconfident. But "it might take much longer" isn't a reason to be complacent. Even at 20 or 30 percent for long timelines, that leaves a majority on it happening soon, and we're nowhere near prepared for that.

r001.rationale: The response mentions a possible paradigm wall and slower algorithmic progress, but does not identify failure to discover sufficiently good AI research ideas despite substantial effort as a cause of a renewed AI winter.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think it's worth being clear about what I mean by "much longer," because a lot hinges on that. If you mean something like AGI doesn't arrive until the 2040s or 2050s or later, I'd put maybe 20, 25 percent on that. Which is not nothing. I don't want to come across as someone who's certain this is happening in the next few years, because I'm not.

But I do think the bulk of my probability mass is in the next ten years, and honestly a lot of it is concentrated in the next three to five. And the reason is pretty simple: the trends. If you look at compute scaling, algorithmic progress, and especially the benchmarks that track how long a task an AI can do autonomously, those have been roughly doubling every few months to a year, depending on how you measure. If you just extrapolate those lines, you get to systems that can do the job of an AI researcher, end to end, sometime around the late 2020s. And once you have that, you get this feedback loop where the AIs are accelerating the research that makes better AIs, and things can move very fast from there.

Now, the scenarios where it takes much longer are basically scenarios where the trends break. Maybe we hit some wall where the current paradigm just doesn't generalize to the messy, long-horizon, real-world stuff. Maybe data runs out and synthetic data doesn't work as well as people hope. Maybe there's a huge compute crunch, or a geopolitical shock, or a regulatory pause. Those are all real possibilities, and I try to take them seriously rather than just hand-wave them away.

But I'd say the honest epistemic situation is that the people who keep saying "it's further away than you think" have been wrong repeatedly over the last five years, and the trend-extrapolation people have been more right than wrong. That should update you. It doesn't mean the extrapolators will keep being right forever, but I don't think you get to put 70 or 80 percent on "much longer" anymore without a pretty specific story about what breaks and why.

So, roughly: a majority chance it's within the decade, a substantial minority chance it's longer, and a fair amount of my own uncertainty is about whether the long-tail scenarios are even coherent, or whether I'm just putting weight there out of a kind of humility reflex.

r001.rationale: The response lists ways trends could break, such as paradigm limits, data shortages, compute constraints, and pauses, but does not mention failing to find sufficiently good AI research ideas despite substantial research effort.

astra-6.text: Maybe 10 or 20%. I think AGI in the next decade is substantially more likely than not, but I wouldn’t be shocked if it took longer. We could discover that some capabilities are much harder to get than they currently look, or that the approaches we’re using hit a wall and we need another major breakthrough. So I put real probability on longer timelines. I just don’t think that’s the scenario we should primarily be planning around.

r001.rationale: The candidate mentions that current approaches could hit a wall and require a breakthrough, but does not identify failure to discover sufficiently good AI research ideas as a cause of a renewed AI winter despite substantial research effort.

sol-6.1.text: I put a substantial probability on that — maybe 20 or 30%. My best guess is that AGI happens within the next decade, but I’m very uncertain. We could run into bottlenecks that turn out to be much harder to overcome than I expect. So I think it’s important to prepare for short timelines without treating them as a certainty.

r001.rationale: The response mentions possible hard-to-overcome bottlenecks, but does not identify failure to find sufficiently good AI research ideas, a renewed AI winter, or substantial research effort.
